study of certain Mesozoic formations in northern Mexico. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 13: 47—56. Rocks of Late Cretaceous, Early Jurassic and Late Triassic age, collected in northern Mexico yield the following pole positions: 169.3°E57.9~N (Cretaceous), 70.7°E76.O°N (?Jurassic) and 119.2°E76.4°N (?Late Trassic). The Triassic and Cretaceous poles are not significantly different from those class-A poles (Hicken et al., 1972) of the North American craton. It is therefore suggested that the North American craton may be traced south as far as 23°N and inferentially a further four degrees (to the Mexican volcanic belt). Proterozoic supracrustal rocks of southwest Greenland and amphibolite dykes intruding the basement possess a thermal remanent magnetisation acquired during slow regional uplift and cooling between 1800 and 1600 m.y. fol- lowing the Ketilidian mobile episode. Most samples from amphibolite dykes (mean palaeomagnetic pole 214°E, 31°N) possess a stable remanence associated with development of hematite during regional thermal metamorphism. Problems in palaeomagnetic synthesis illustrated by results from Permo-Triassic dolerites in Guyana. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 16: 277—284. Relatively consistent palaeomagnetic results have been obtained after alternating field demagnetization of samples from seven of eight dolerite dykes (ten sites) intruding the basement shield in Guyana. Results from five of these dykes (seven sites, 33 samples) give an average site-pole at 63°S, 138°W, k = 24.6, ~ = 12.4°. Despite K—Ar ages ranging from 262 to 675 m.y., the good grouping suggests that these dykes are generally contemporaneous, and they are judged to be Permo-Triassic. The remaining two dykes have distinct, apparently Precambrian, magnetizations. The geology, which has been mapped at a scale of one inch to four miles by Baer (1967), is complex and difficult to interpret because the area is underlain mainly by various ages of granitic plutonic rocks of similar composition with very few time-markers (Table 1) . However, there are numerous dykes, a few plutons , and some flows of basic composition in the area and it w as thought that paleomagnetism could help in classifying and dating the various periods of intrusion. Funda­ mentally, the procedure consists in deriving the pole position from the stable primary remanence direction of the pluton, dyke swarm or lava sequence, and to compare it with pole positions derived from North American rock formations of known age (e. g. de Boer, 1967; Larochelle, 1967 and 1968a). carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: map-areas span the Coast Mountains in west-central British Columbia (Fig. 1). The geology, which has been mapped at a scale of one inch to four miles by Baer (1967), is complex and difficult to interpret because the area is underlain mainly by various ages of granitic plutonic rocks of similar composition with very few time-markers (Table 1) . However, there are numerous dykes, a few plutons , and some flows of basic composition in the area and it w as thought that paleomagnetism could help in classifying and dating the various periods of intrusion. Funda­ mentally, the procedure consists in deriving the pole position from the stable primary remanence direction of the pluton, dyke swarm or lava sequence, and to compare it with pole positions derived from North American rock formations of known age (e. g. de Boer, 1967; Larochelle, 1967 and 1968a). The rock units sampled are underlined in Table 1 and listed here in chronologic order starting with the oldest: (1) greens tone complex, (2) gabb­ roic intrusives, (3) green andesitic dykes, (4) granodiorite intrusives , (5) blue porphyritic dykes, (6) basaltic flows, and (7) brown basaltic dykes. This position indi­ cates an Upper Tertiary or Quaternary age of remanence acquisition. The presence of reversed remanence, the fresh appearance of the rocks and their geological relationships indicate that these dykes retain their primary TRM . The presence of reversed remanence also indicates that intrusion of the dykes occurred over a sufficiently long period of time (105 to 107 years) for the earth's magnetic field to reverse its polarity. This evidence favours the averaging of any bias in the pole position caused through secular variation, and an Upper Miocene to Pleistocene rather than Holocene age of intrusion. Page V 1 3 3 3 8 8 8 10 10 11 11 12 12 14 2 4 5 6 7 vi 9 - V - ABSTRACT The Coast Mountains are underlain mostly by a complex assemblage of granitic plutonic rocks with few time -markers. The paleomagnetism of 533 specimens from 70 sites representing several geological units of basic igneous origin in the Bella Coola-Laredo Sound map-areas was studied to assess their value as time-markers. The stable partial NRM of the speci­ mens was isolated by alt~rnating field demagnetization. Only 31 sites yielded remanence data of sufficient stability and homogeneity to be considered acceptable according to preset criteria. These data confirm and in part refine the geological time-scale established for the map-areas by reconnai­ ssance mapping. Page V 1 3 3 3 8 8 8 10 10 11 11 12 12 14 2 4 5 6 7 vi 9 - V - ABSTRACT The Coast Mountains are underlain mostly by a complex assemblage of granitic plutonic rocks with few time -markers. The paleomagnetism of 533 specimens from 70 sites representing several geological units of basic igneous origin in the Bella Coola-Laredo Sound map-areas was studied to assess their value as time-markers. The stable partial NRM of the speci­ mens was isolated by alt~rnating field demagnetization. Only 31 sites yielded remanence data of sufficient stability and homogeneity to be considered acceptable according to preset criteria. These data confirm and in part refine the geological time-scale established for the map-areas by reconnai­ ssance mapping. Therefore, it appears that these gabbro plutons were intruded before the Cretaceous as close in time to the Triassic-Early Jurassic as possible which combined with the paleontological evidence - 10 - suggests a Middle or Upper Jurassic age, and that they retain their primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) without significant subsequent meta­ morphic alteration or tectonic rotation. A gabbroic dyke (*2)* cuts one of the Jurassic gabbroic plutons and another one occurs on the extreme eastern side of the Coast Mountains. Both dykes are in fairly stable tectonic areas, and both are composed of massive and apparently unaltered gabbro. They yielded acceptable and consistent paleomagnetic data. The resulting pole position (160.1°E., 55. 0°N.) diverges from the Triassic pole positions and the earth's present magnetic pole, and aligns most closely with reliable Cretaceous pole positions (Fig. 2a). This evidence, admittedly based on only two sites, is consistent with a Cretaceous period of intrusion and with the dykes retaining a primary TRM. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: map-areas span the Coast Mountains in west-central British Columbia (Fig. 1). The geology, which has been mapped at a scale of one inch to four miles by Baer (1967), is complex and difficult to interpret because the area is underlain mainly by various ages of granitic plutonic rocks of similar composition with very few time-markers (Table 1) . However, there are numerous dykes, a few plutons , and some flows of basic composition in the area and it w as thought that paleomagnetism could help in classifying and dating the various periods of intrusion. Funda­ mentally, the procedure consists in deriving the pole position from the stable primary remanence direction of the pluton, dyke swarm or lava sequence, and to compare it with pole positions derived from North American rock formations of known age (e. g. de Boer, 1967; Larochelle, 1967 and 1968a). The rock units sampled are underlined in Table 1 and listed here in chronologic order starting with the oldest: (1) greens tone complex, (2) gabb­ roic intrusives, (3) green andesitic dykes, (4) granodiorite intrusives , (5) blue porphyritic dykes, (6) basaltic flows, and (7) brown basaltic dykes. This indicates that the two con- tinents could twice been parts of a single plate, once during the Middle Precambrian (1 900— 1 300 My) and once from the Silurian to the Triassic (McElhinny, 1973). Further studies will throw more light on the problem but as a working hypothesis one could assume that (2 200 My) the two landmasses were widely separated prior to the Svecokarelian orogeny, as is indicated by the differences in climatical conditions and paleomagnetic orienta- tion, but that they were forced together during the Penokean-Svecokarelian (1 900 My) move- ments. This intimate connection might have lasted a considerable length of time (about 600 My) and terminated during the Jotnian-Macken- zie episode. Palaeomagnetic investigation Approximately five block samples per flow or dyke were oriented in the field. From eaeh of these a single core was drilled in the laboratory. After measurement of NRM (natural remanent magnetization using a FOSTEn [1966] slow speed fluxgate spinner), a single core per igneous unit was progressively demagnetized in an alternating magnetic field. The maximum field strength applied, 600 oe, was reached in four stages (Fig. 3). Examination of plots of intensity against declination and inclination show that in the majority of cases the secondary component of magnetization is small, and removed in fields of either 150 oe or 300 oe. The remaining samples were then all demagnetized at these two field strengths. The direction adopted as the best representation of the field at the time of intrusion or extrusion was that at which the site mean had the lowest a95 and highest K values (see InveNt et al., 1961). These site mean directions of magnetization are shown in Fig. 4 a, b and the data is listed in table 1 a, b. Palaeomagnetic investigation Approximately five block samples per flow or dyke were oriented in the field. From eaeh of these a single core was drilled in the laboratory. After measurement of NRM (natural remanent magnetization using a FOSTEn [1966] slow speed fluxgate spinner), a single core per igneous unit was progressively demagnetized in an alternating magnetic field. The maximum field strength applied, 600 oe, was reached in four stages (Fig. 3). Examination of plots of intensity against declination and inclination show that in the majority of cases the secondary component of magnetization is small, and removed in fields of either 150 oe or 300 oe. The remaining samples were then all demagnetized at these two field strengths. The direction adopted as the best representation of the field at the time of intrusion or extrusion was that at which the site mean had the lowest a95 and highest K values (see InveNt et al., 1961). These site mean directions of magnetization are shown in Fig. 4 a, b and the data is listed in table 1 a, b. INTRODUCTION The present knowledge about the Late Paleozoic reversals of the geomagnetic field (Valencio and Mitchell, 1972), generally known as the Kiaman Magnetic Interval or Late Paleozoic Interval of Reversed Geomagnetic Polarity, allow us to assign an age according with the polarity of their primary magnetic remanences to those rocks formed within the interval Upper Carboniferous-Lower Triassic. Obviously, this is only valid for those rocks whose Upper Paleozoic-Lower Mesozoic ages are supported by clas­ sical geological (paleontology, paleobotany, stratigraphy, etc.) data and holders of mag­ netic remanences originated during their formation. Abstract Paleomagnetic investigations of the Iranian-Afghanian Plate -- well defined by geo- logical history and seismotectonics yield following pole positions: Permian 42W 8 N, lower Cretaceous 48 W 65 N, lower Tertiary 100 W 75 N, upper Tertiary 180 W 78 N. These paleomagnetic results, supported by fracture zones and magnetic anomalies of the Indian Ocean floor make it possible to reconstruct the plate movement from the eastern margin of Gondwana to the southern margin of Laurasia. After the prepermian sep- aration from Gondwana the Afghan-Iranian Plate moves northward rotating anticlockwise and collides with the Russian Plate until lower Cretaceous time. Earlier than lower Tertiary the Arabian Plate reaches at the SW margin of the Afghan-Iranian Plate. J. D. A. Piper, Sub-department of Geophysics, Oliver Lodge Laboratory, University of Liverpool, Oxford Street, Liverpool L69 3BX, England. April 16th, 1976. The Precambrian Ilimaussaq complex is one of a number of peralkaline instrusions within the Gardar igneous province of south Green­ land, but is unique in the high degree of peralkalinity and enrichment in such elements as Zr and Cl. This paper reports palaeomagnetic results from a collection of syenites from the margin and agpaites (highly undersaturated· syenites) from the interior of the pluton. Such a study has become particularly relevant in the light of detailed geochronological work on the com­ plex by Moorbath et al. (1960) and Blaxland et al. (1976). Geology The geology of the Ilimaussaq intrusion is described in a comprehensive memoir by Us­ sing (1912), and more recent accounts include those by Ferguson (1964, 1970), Hamilton (1964), Ss,Srensen et al. (1969) and Bohse et al. (1971); these descriptions reference many other more specialised studies of the complex. Th.e earliest phase is a

d more recent accounts include those by Ferguson (1964, 1970), Hamilton (1964), Ss,Srensen et al. (1969) and Bohse et al. (1971); these descriptions reference many other more specialised studies of the complex. Th.e earliest phase is an augite syenite which forms a marginal envelope around the side of the intrusion at its southern margin and also 7 D.g.F. 25 occurs at the uppermost levels. The bulk of this unit is medium to coarse grained but includes a chilled facies at the margin; ne­ pheline occurs further from the contact with the country rock and local mineral banding with steep inward dips is also observed. Palaeomagnetic sites 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 comprise a single traverse across the syenite beginning near the contact with country rocks on the east side of Kangerdluarssuak; site 6 is close to the contact on west side of the fjord (fig. 1). Within the intrusion, rhythmically layered kakortokites (eudialyte-bearing nepheline syen­ ites) represent the deepest exposed part of the intrusion, and Bohse et al. (1971) have recog­ nised and mapped 29 major layers comprising arfvedsonite, eudialyte and feldspar with nepheline. a stable secondary magnetic moment and arguments are given for believing this to have been recently acquired. It therefore follows that haematite is more mobile in permeable sandstones than has generally been thought. The results suggest that the Jurassic palaeomagnetic pole for North America, based largely on preliminary work by Runcorn and Collinson & Runcorn from the same formation and similar red-bed lithologies, is based on rocks with a present-day component of magnetization. The virtual poles reported by DeBoer or Helsley & Steiner may be the best representations of the North American Jurassic palaeomagnetic pole position. Geophys. J. R. mtr. SOC. (1976) 44, 161-175. Palaeomagnetism of the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone from South-western Utah Allen H. Johnson (Received 1975 June 18)* A combination of petrographic and magnetic studies indicates that the Navajo Sandstone carries a stable secondary magnetic moment and arguments are given for believing this to have been recently acquired. It therefore follows that haematite is more mobile in permeable sandstones than has generally been thought. The results suggest that the Jurassic palaeomagnetic pole for North America, based largely on preliminary work by Runcorn and Collinson & Runcorn from the same formation and similar red-bed lithologies, is based on rocks with a present-day component of magnetization. The virtual poles reported by DeBoer or Helsley & Steiner may be the best representations of the North American Jurassic palaeomagnetic pole position. A petrographic study indicates that the investigation of the Navajo Sandstone as a means of detailing the behaviour and detailing a part of the polar wandering curve for North America is not feasible. However, a residuum of the original Jurassic component may be seen in the reversely magnetized sites. There probably exist similar residue in the normally magnetized sites, but these Jurass

A petrographic study indicates that the investigation of the Navajo Sandstone as a means of detailing the behaviour and detailing a part of the polar wandering curve for North America is not feasible. However, a residuum of the original Jurassic component may be seen in the reversely magnetized sites. Introduction The investigation of the Lower Jurassic Navajo Sandstone of western North America was begun with the object of providing reliable palaeomagnetic data for this interval of geologic time, and to detail as closely as possible the behaviour of the geomagnetic field. Recently attempts have been made to identify a Jurassic magnetic anomaly sequence in oceanographic work without any real indication from palaeo- magnetism of how the field actually behaved (Vogt et ul. 1970; Larsen & Chase 1972). Palaeomagnetic control for the Jurassic is poor although McElhinny & Burek (1971) have attempted to combine palaeomagnetic results from the literature to derive a palaeomagnetic reversal chronology for the whole of the Mesozoic. Since most palaeomagnetic work has not been based on closely-spaced stratigraphic sampling, there may be many reversals that have not been reported. Conclusions Lower Carboniferous limestones in Ireland carry two stable magnetic components, one in the Permian and one in the significantly different Lower Carboni- ferous field direction. [3], and also on Upper Tertiary volcanic Cocks in east Sicily [2,3]. In this paper pa- laeomagnetic results for Upper Cretaceous and Middle Jurassic volcanic rocks in west Sicily are reported. An analysis,of paleomagnetic remanence data shows that two units within the St. Joseph Till were sampled, although it has not been possible to find a consistent stratigraphic break from field examinations. These two units give separate virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) positions of lat. 67.1" N, long. 297.8" W and lat. 65. lo N, long. 220.6" W. Remanence data from varved clays for the Walkerton area, which were deposited at about the same time as the St. Joseph Till, gave a VGP position close to the mean of all remanence results from the St. Joseph Till. s the St. Joseph Till, gave a VGP position close to the mean of all remanence results from the St. Joseph Till. A spruce log extracted from the till was dated at 13 100 -c 110 y B.P. (GSC-2213), which is consistent with the time of the Port Huron ice advance. Sampling was carried out using a field coring drill (Doell and Cox 1967) with which 3 to 7 cores per flow were drilled (because of difficulty in drilling, three flows in the Castles section are represented by less than 3 cores). Cores were oriented using a sun compass wherever possible and by sighting on geographic features whose true bearing had been determined using the sun and topographic maps. Measurements were done on a 5 Hz spinner magnetometer (Foster 1966). Alternating field demagnetization studies were carried out using magnetic cleaning apparatus similar to that described by McElhinny (1966). Detailed stepwise a.f. cleaning up to more than 2000 Oe was done on 24 pilot specimens from 13 of the Wait Creek flows. All specimens showed good end-points below 380 Oe peak a.f. ; the relative change in intensity at this field, JIJ,, was between 0.3 and 0.8 (Fig. 2). It was therefore decided to apply blanket treatment of 380 Oe to one specimen from each of the other cores in the section. For either of the two sampling assumptions described above, this probability is less than 0.5%. This leads to two possible conclusions. Either the number of field excur- sions occurring in the time period sampled was very high (or perhaps very local), or the results were due to fortuitous sampling, the probability of which is very low. The latter case is, however, intuitively more appealing. Since the age of the Wrangell Volcanics is near the Gilbert Reversed-Gauss Normal Epoch boundary, the geomagnetic field behavior re- corded may have occurred during polarity transi- tions. Because of the stratigraphic relationships between the sections sampled, two different polarity transitions are required: The Wait Creek section would have sampled the 'tail end' of a reversed-normal transition while the strati- graphically higher Castles section would repre- sent either a time near the beginning of a normal- reversed transition or a time near the end of a reversed-normal transition. No rocks of reversed polarity have been sampled in the Wrangell Volcanics. Earth Sci.. 13.476489(1976) Introduction Polyphase magnetization is the phenomenon whereby a rock unit may contain several different magnetizations, each corresponding to the geo- magnetic field at various times during the history of the rock unit. These magnetizations may be present in different oxide phases, or in different grain-size ranges of the same oxide phase. They can be separated by chemical leaching, which progressively removes the finer grain-size frac- tions and the magnetizations they carry; by al- ternating field (AF) demagnetization, which pro- gressively removes the magnetizations of lower remanent coercive force; or by thermal demag- netization, which progressively removes the magnetizations with lower blocking tempera- tures. The phenomenon of polyphase magnetiza- tion is analogous to polyphase deformation in metamorphic rocks, which is indicative of a complex metamorphic history, and to the occur- rence of a spread of apparent dates obtained in geochronological studies, which is indicative of a complex thermal history. Earth Sci.. 13.476489(1976) Introduction Polyphase magnetization is the phenomenon whereby a rock unit may contain several different magnetizations, each corresponding to the geo- magnetic field at various times during the history of the rock unit. These magnetizations may be present in different oxide phases, or in different grain-size ranges of the same oxide phase. They can be separated by chemical leaching, which progressively removes the finer grain-size frac- tions and the magnetizations they carry; by al- ternating field (AF) demagnetization, which pro- gressively removes the magnetizations of lower remanent coercive force; or by thermal demag- netization, which progressively removes the magnetizations with lower blocking tempera- tures. The phenomenon of polyphase magnetiza- tion is analogous to polyphase deformation in metamorphic rocks, which is indicative of a complex metamorphic history, and to the occur- rence of a spread of apparent dates obtained in geochronological studies, which is indicative of a complex thermal history.
